content.text: Static Electricity
Introduction

Have you ever experienced a small shock when touching a door handle after walking across a carpet? Or noticed your hair standing up after removing a woollen jumper? These everyday phenomena are caused by static electricity—electric charge that builds up on objects and stays in place rather than flowing. Understanding static electricity is the first step to understanding all electrical phenomena.
Key Concept:
Static electricity is caused by an imbalance of electric charges on an object. Only electrons move during charging — protons remain fixed in the nucleus.
Key Concepts
Electric Charge
Electric charge
is a fundamental property of matter. There are two types:
Positive charge (+):
carried by protons
Negative charge (−):
carried by electrons
Most objects are electrically
neutral
—they have equal numbers of protons and electrons.
Charging by Friction
When two different materials are rubbed together:
Electrons transfer from one material to the other
One material gains electrons (becomes negative)
One material loses electrons (becomes positive)
Important:
Protons do NOT move. Only electrons transfer.

attrs.alt: Electrostatic charging by friction showing electron transfer between materials

content.text: Examples of Charging

| Materials Rubbed | Result |
|------------------|--------|
| Polythene rod + cloth | Rod becomes negative (gains electrons) |
| Acetate rod + cloth | Rod becomes positive (loses electrons) |
| Balloon + hair | Balloon negative, hair positive |
| Feet + carpet | Person becomes charged |
Laws of Electrostatics
Like charges repel:
positive repels positive, negative repels negative
Unlike charges attract:
positive attracts negative
This is why charged balloons stick to walls (inducing opposite charge) and why your hair stands up (strands with same charge repel each other).
Electrostatic Phenomena
Attraction of Uncharged Objects
A charged object can attract an uncharged object through
induction
Charged object brought near neutral object
Electrons in neutral object are attracted or repelled
One side becomes slightly positive, other slightly negative
Net attraction because closer charges exert stronger force

content.text: Electric Discharge
Discharge
occurs when charge suddenly flows from one place to another:
Static shock when touching metal
Lightning (giant spark between cloud and ground)
Sparks from removing synthetic clothing
Lightning
Lightning is a dramatic example of static discharge:
Ice crystals in clouds rub together
Charge builds up (typically negative at cloud base)
This induces positive charge on ground
When voltage is high enough, air becomes conducting
Massive current flows as a lightning bolt
Exam Tip:
When explaining electrostatic induction, always state that the closer opposite charges experience a stronger force than the farther like charges, resulting in a net attraction.
Dangers of Static Electricity
Sparks and Explosions
Static sparks can ignite flammable materials:
Petrol stations: fuel vapour can ignite
Flour mills and grain stores: dust explosions
Operating theatres: anaesthetic gases
Solutions
Earthing (grounding):
Connecting objects to the ground allows charge to flow safely away.
Anti-static measures:
Fuel tankers have earthing straps
Workers wear anti-static wristbands
Floors are made conducting
Humid air reduces charge build-up
Useful Applications
Electrostatic Precipitators
Remove pollution from smoke:
Smoke passes through charged metal grid
Particles become charged
Attracted to oppositely charged collecting plates
Clean air exits chimney
Photocopiers and Laser Printers
Drum given uniform charge
Light removes charge where image is white
Toner (charged powder) sticks to remaining charged areas
Toner transferred to paper and heated to fix
Spray Painting
Paint droplets given electric charge
Object to be painted is earthed (or oppositely charged)
Paint attracted evenly to all surfaces
Less waste, even coating, reaches awkward areas
Crop Spraying
Similar principle to spray painting—charged pesticide droplets are attracted to plants.
Real-World Link:
Electrostatic spray painting wastes less paint and gives a more even coating because charged droplets are attracted to all surfaces of the object, including hard-to-reach areas.
Worked Examples
Example 1:
A polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. Explain what has happened to the electrons.
Solution:

Electrons have transferred from the cloth to the polythene rod. The rod now has more electrons than protons, giving it a net negative charge. The cloth has lost electrons and now has more protons than electrons, so it's positively charged.
Example 2:
Why does a charged balloon stick to a wall?
Solution:
The balloon has excess negative charge
When brought near the wall, the negative charges in the wall are repelled
This leaves the near surface of the wall slightly positive
The positive surface of the wall attracts the negative balloon
The balloon sticks due to electrostatic attraction
Example 3:
Explain why earthing a fuel tanker prevents explosions.
Solution:

As fuel flows through pipes, friction can cause charge to build up on the tanker. If this charge accumulates, it could discharge as a spark, igniting fuel vapour. The earthing strap provides a conducting path to the ground, allowing charge to flow away safely and preventing dangerous build-up.
Common Misconceptions
"Positive charges move when objects are charged"
— Only electrons (negative) move. Positive charge appears when electrons are removed.
"Static electricity is different from current electricity"
— It's the same phenomenon; static refers to charge that isn't flowing, while current is charge in motion.
"Charged objects attract everything"
— Charged objects attract opposite charges and can attract neutral objects through induction, but they repel like charges.
"Static only happens in dry weather"
— Static occurs all the time, but humid air allows charge to leak away more easily, making effects less noticeable.
"Lightning conductors attract lightning"
— They provide a safe path for discharge but don't increase the likelihood of a strike in that location.
Practice Problems
Explain what happens to the electrons when a glass rod is rubbed with silk, given that the rod becomes positively charged.
Describe what happens when two charged polythene rods are brought close together, and explain why.
Explain why a charged plastic comb can pick up small pieces of uncharged paper.
Explain why aircraft have static discharge wicks on their wings.
Describe how an electrostatic precipitator removes particles from smoke.
Explain why hospital operating theatres are kept humid.
Describe the process by which a person becomes charged while walking across a nylon carpet, and explain why they feel a shock when touching a metal door handle.
Summary
Electric charge: positive (protons) and negative (electrons)
Charging by friction: electrons transfer between materials
Like charges repel, unlike charges attract
Charged objects attract neutral objects through induction
Dangers: sparks can cause fires and explosions
Safety: earthing allows charge to flow away safely
Applications: precipitators, photocopiers, spray painting
Only electrons move—protons stay fixed in nuclei
Answer Key
Electrons transfer from the glass rod to the silk.
The glass loses electrons, giving it more protons than electrons and a net positive charge. The silk gains those electrons and becomes negatively charged. (recall & application)
The rods repel each other.
Both polythene rods are negatively charged (they gain electrons when rubbed). Like charges repel, so the rods push apart. (recall & reasoning)
The comb attracts the paper by electrostatic induction.

The charged comb causes charge separation in the neutral paper -- the near side acquires opposite charge to the comb. The closer opposite charges exert a stronger force than the farther like charges, producing a net attraction. (reasoning)
Static discharge wicks allow charge to leak away safely.

Friction from airflow causes charge to build up on wings. Without wicks, a sudden spark could damage electronics or ignite fuel vapour. The pointed wicks let charge dissipate gradually into the air. (application & reasoning)
Smoke passes through a charged metal grid, so particles become charged. They are then attracted to oppositely charged collecting plates, where they stick. Clean air exits the chimney.
(recall & description)
Humid air allows static charge to leak away more easily.
In operating theatres, flammable anaesthetic gases could be ignited by a static spark, so keeping the air humid prevents dangerous charge build-up. (reasoning)

Walking on the carpet charges the person by friction -- electrons transfer between feet and carpet. The person accumulates excess charge. When they touch the metal handle (a conductor), the charge rapidly discharges through the handle to earth, and this sudden flow of current is felt as a shock.
(application & reasoning)
